source_title: Use of drones; Federal Aviation Administration requirements
uas_topic: Federal compliance; operating requirements; model aircraft
regulated_party: Any person using a drone, including law-enforcement agencies
requirement_type: Mandatory compliance with applicable FAA requirements; stated legislative intent for model-aircraft community guidelines
summary: Section 4623 provides that any drone use by any person, including a law-enforcement agency, must comply with all applicable FAA requirements and guidelines. It separately states legislative intent that a person using a model aircraft, as defined in the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012, operate according to community-based-organization guidelines such as the Academy of Model Aeronautics safety code. The section creates no separate Vermont commercial UAS registration, pilot credential, or operating permit.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Vermont Legislature statute page
notes: The online statutes state that they include the 2025 session; the 2026 session was separately checked for enacted UAS changes.

geographic_scope: Statewide; use by defined law-enforcement agencies and persons or entities acting on their behalf
uas_topic: Law enforcement; surveillance; warrants; data minimization; biometrics
regulated_party: Defined law-enforcement agencies and persons or entities acting on their behalf
regulated_activity: Investigative, prosecutorial, search-and-rescue, damage-assessment, and other public-safety drone use
requirement_type: General prohibition with warrant, noncriminal-purpose, and judicial-exception paths; data limits and exclusion remedy
permit_or_approval_required: Rule 41 warrant or a stated alternative is required for covered investigative use
commercial_operator_relevance: High for law-enforcement clients and contractors
summary: Section 4622 generally prohibits a defined law-enforcement agency, including a person or entity acting for one, from using a drone or drone-acquired information to investigate, detect, or prosecute crime except under stated conditions. Permitted paths include noncriminal purposes such as search and rescue or damage assessment, a Vermont Rule 41 warrant, or a judicially recognized warrant exception. The statute restricts collection outside the surveillance target, limits biometric matching, requires a warrant within 48 hours after exigent use, and makes improperly gathered evidence inadmissible.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Vermont Legislature statute page
notes: Chapter 205 defines law-enforcement agency to include a person or entity acting on behalf of a listed agency.

geographic_scope: Statewide; law-enforcement agencies that used a drone during the prior 12 months
issuing_authority: Vermont General Assembly and Department of Public Safety
revision_date: 2026 Act 157 confirmed continuation outside general report sunset
uas_topic: Public reporting; deployments; incidental collection; cost; funding
regulated_party: Law-enforcement agencies using drones and the Department of Public Safety
regulated_activity: Reporting drone use, results, incidental collection, program cost, and funding
permit_or_approval_required: Annual submission to DPS and legislative reporting are required; no private operator application stated
summary: Section 4624 requires a law-enforcement agency that used a drone during the prior 12 months to report annually to the Department of Public Safety. Required information includes deployments and rationales, information collected, investigations and arrests aided, incidental collection involving nontarget persons or places, program cost, and funding source. DPS then reports the collected information to specified legislative committees. Act 157 of 2026 lists this report among reports exempted from a general statutory report-sunset mechanism; it does not create a new private-operator duty.
verification_status: Verified against current statute and enacted 2026 Act 157
notes: The contractor implication arises only when acting for a covered agency or supplying information needed for its report.

geographic_scope: Correctional facilities and readily recognizable or identified surrounding correctional property
source_title: Correctional facilities; use of drones prohibited; civil penalty
uas_topic: Corrections; overflight; commercial exception; consent; notice
regulated_party: Any drone operator, subject to enumerated exceptions
regulated_activity: Knowingly operating over correctional facilities or recognizable or identified surrounding property
requirement_type: Civil prohibition with commercial, consent, agency, and emergency exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: Written consent or prior notice applies to specified paths; qualifying commercial FAA-compliant use is separately excepted
summary: Section 4625 prohibits knowingly operating a drone over a correctional facility or surrounding property readily recognizable as correctional property or reasonably identified by fencing or signs. A violation carries a civil penalty up to $500. The prohibition does not apply to the Department of Corrections, written consent from the supervising officer, or a commercial-purpose operation conducted in compliance with an FAA authorization, rule, or exemption. Buildings and General Services and its contractors, law enforcement, and specified emergency users receive separate exceptions with prior notice.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Vermont Legislature statute page
notes: Do not convert the commercial exception into a conclusion about live federal airspace or facility permission.

source_title: Drones over private property; surveillance and consent
uas_topic: Private property; privacy; surveillance; imagery; written consent; recreational altitude
regulated_party: Any drone operator, subject to utility and law-enforcement exceptions
regulated_activity: Low recreational overflight and recording private property or people with intent to conduct privacy-violating surveillance
requirement_type: Civil prohibition with written-consent standard, privacy presumption, definitions, and exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: Prior written owner or occupant consent is material under the stated conditions
summary: Section 4626 prohibits recreational drone flight below 100 feet over private real property without prior written owner consent. Separately, it prohibits any person from using a drone, without prior written owner or occupant consent, to record imagery of private property or its owner or occupant with intent to conduct surveillance violating a reasonable expectation of privacy. The section defines surveillance, presumes privacy when a person is not observable from a lawful ground-level position, sets civil penalties, and excepts qualifying utility reliability/resiliency work and legitimate law-enforcement use.
verification_status: Verified directly against current statute and 2024 Act 161
notes: The below-100-foot rule in subsection (a) is expressly limited to hobby or recreational purposes; subsection (b) is not.

geographic_scope: Retail transactions involving federally registrable drones
uas_topic: Equipment sales; purchaser notice; private-property rules
regulated_party: Persons engaged in the business of selling drones
regulated_activity: Selling a drone required to be registered by the U.S. Department of Transportation
requirement_type: Written purchaser-notice requirement with civil penalty
permit_or_approval_required: No agency approval stated; written notice to purchaser required
commercial_operator_relevance: Moderate for direct sellers; low for ordinary operators
summary: A person engaged in the business of selling drones must give each purchaser of a drone required to be registered by the U.S. Department of Transportation written notice about § 4626(a) and (b), which address low recreational flight and surveillance over private property without prior written consent. A violation is subject to a civil penalty of up to $50 for a first violation and $250 for a later violation. The provision regulates seller disclosure; it does not establish an approved-product list or make the purchaser's aircraft ineligible for commercial work.
verification_status: Verified directly against current statute and 2024 Act 161
notes: Relevant to an AEC firm only if it is engaged in the business of selling covered drones, not merely buying or disposing of fleet equipment.

source_title: Drones; dangerous or deadly weapons and projectiles
regulated_activity: Equipping a drone with a dangerous or deadly weapon or firing a projectile from a drone
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition punishable by imprisonment, fine, or both
summary: Section 4018 prohibits any person from equipping a drone with a dangerous or deadly weapon or firing a projectile from a drone. The statute incorporates chapter 205's drone definition and § 4016's dangerous-or-deadly-weapon definition. A violation may be punished by imprisonment for not more than one year, a fine of not more than $1,000, or both. The provision does not state an exception for ordinary commercial work, testing, public agencies, or a nonweapon payload that could be characterized as a projectile.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Vermont Legislature statute page
notes: Payload-release missions require careful classification because the text separately prohibits firing a projectile.

uas_topic: Wildlife; hunting; locating; surveillance; driving; harassment
regulated_party: Any person using a drone or UAV in relation to taking wildlife; qualified personnel exception
regulated_activity: Taking or assisting the taking of wildlife with UAS, including locating, surveilling, driving, or harassing
permit_or_approval_required: Applicable permits may be required for qualified personnel; no general UAS permit stated
commercial_operator_relevance: Moderate near wildlife or hunting activity
summary: Fish and Wildlife Board Rule § 20 prohibits taking or attempting to take wild animals with a UAV. It also prohibits using a drone or UAV to locate, surveil, or assist in locating or surveilling a wild animal for the purpose of taking it, and to drive or harass wildlife or otherwise assist a take. The rule does not apply to qualified personnel carrying out lawful duties in compliance with applicable state and federal regulations and permits, and it does not alter other aircraft or UAS compliance requirements.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Vermont Fish and Wildlife rule published by the Legislature
notes: The locating and surveillance clauses require a purpose related to taking wildlife; harassment is also separately prohibited.

geographic_scope: FPR state parks, forests, lands, and facilities as defined in the procedure
issuing_authority: Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation
source_title: Drone Usage on FPR State Lands Procedure
citation: FPR Procedure dated Jan. 29, 2025; CVR 12-020-009 I.17
status: Current official procedure and property-use requirement
binding_level: Binding property-use requirement and official procedure
uas_topic: State lands; commercial use; Special Use Permit; License; insurance; resources
regulated_party: Persons launching and landing drones on covered FPR lands; stated agency and emergency exceptions
regulated_activity: Drone use originating and terminating on state park or forest lands and facilities
requirement_type: Written Commissioner approval through Special Use Permit or License; case-specific review
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — online Special Use Permit or License application for covered commercial use
summary: FPR's January 2025 procedure requires written Commissioner permission through a Special Use Permit or License before a person launches and lands a drone on state park or forest lands or facilities. Commercial operations require a permit or license, requested through the online state-lands application. Regional staff review completeness, insurance, payment, mission alignment, parcel management, conflicts with public uses, resource impacts, safety, liability, and prior performance; approval is discretionary and may include time or day restrictions. Emergency response, certain state-agency work, qualified ANR staff, and lawful law-enforcement activity have stated exceptions.
verification_status: Verified directly against the signed official January 29, 2025 procedure
notes: The procedure distinguishes FAA-regulated overflight from launch and landing on FPR property and states that FPR is not obligated to approve an application.
